job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Pedro Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in electrical engineering with a focus on telecoms and signal processing. I live with my parents in Ferrow and take the train in, forty minutes each way, which is where I read papers. In the evenings I call my fiancée Lucia, who's a nurse on nights this month, and we argue happily about the wedding budget. My father was an electrician at a factory that closed, so he knows how fast a good job can go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go. Hard work and skills still count, and no machine is going to marry us. I'd tell friends to ignore the noise and keep building a life, because that's what my father did and it mostly worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, plateau is a good outcome but I'm not relaxed. I have a heavy loan, about a week of money saved and not many telecom or electrical firms around Ferrow. Northlink, where I interned, hired two graduates last year and had two hundred applicants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and apply to Northlink and every electrical firm within an hour on the train. I'd ask my father's old foreman, Mr Brandt, whether the contractors he knows are hiring. And I'd keep my wedding plan small, because we won't have money for the big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, steady. I'm grateful, in a way, that the world isn't being turned upside down while I'm trying to start a life. But I'd be lying if I said the loan didn't wake me at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Lucia are planning a wedding. How does that change the way you read all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It made everything smaller. My mother stopped her classes and started cleaning houses, and my father took temp jobs. We've never been poor, but we count everything. That's why I want a stable job and a quiet wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your father's factory closed. What did that do to the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd push the date back a year, and I'd feel like I let her down. She'd say it doesn't matter, but it does to me. I want to do it properly, and I think a lot of men my age feel that.

say: I'd say **hard work and skills** still count, and no machine is going to marry us.
I'd tell friends to ignore the noise and **keep building a life**.
think: A plateau is good, but I carry a **heavy loan** and few telecom firms are near Ferrow.
Northlink had **two hundred applicants** for two graduate places last year.
do: Apply to **Northlink** and every electrical firm within an hour by train.
Ask Mr Brandt (my father's old foreman) whether **contractors** he knows are hiring.
feel: **Steady and grateful**, but the loan still wakes me at night.
S0.quote: I want to do it properly, and I think a lot of men my age feel that.
fieldNote: Family pride and the **wedding** shape his money worries.
His father's factory closure taught him how fast a good job can go.
Faith in hard work, with a very practical job hunt.

steps.text: Apply to Northlink and every electrical firm within an hour's train ride
Ask Mr Brandt about contractors who are hiring
Plan a small wedding with Lucia on a fixed budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will have to work harder and smarter, and employers should hire and train young people, not just buy software. I don't want handouts, I want work. But I'd say plainly that firms that cut entry jobs need to offer apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my first rung is in danger. Network monitoring, test scripts and report writing, which are what juniors do, are moving to software. I think firms hire half as many juniors and expect each to do twice as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, since I already use them now and then and they're improving. I'd also aim for jobs with a field side, like installing and fault repair on masts, because those need a person. And I'd start a small savings pot, a hundred pounds a month, once I'm earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious. I'm not scared, but I'd be walking carefully. There's a plan in my head with a lot of if-thens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of telecom work does Steady Disruption change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut red tape for firms that hire young people, pay for apprenticeships and let people keep what they earn. I don't want a government that tells me what to feel, just one that stays out of the way of a man trying to start work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think a good response looks like from a government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Network monitoring, written reports and fault logging. At Northlink the juniors did those on a rota. Now there's software that does the first pass and a senior checks it.

say: I'd say employers should **hire and train** young people, not just buy software.
I'd say I don't want **handouts**, I want work.
think: The **first rung** is in danger, because network monitoring and report writing are moving to software.
Firms may hire **half as many** juniors and expect each to do twice as much.
do: Use **AI tools** more, since they're getting better.
Aim for **field jobs** like mast installation and fault repair.
Start a **£100 a month** savings pot once I'm earning.
feel: **Cautious**, walking carefully with a plan full of if-thens.
S1.quote: I don't want a government that tells me what to feel, just one that stays out of the way of a man trying to start work.
fieldNote: Wants **work, not handouts**, but asks firms to carry some of the cost.
Steady adopter: uses AI more as it proves itself.
Field jobs on masts are his answer to the shrinking junior desk.

steps.text: Practise AI tools for scripting and network analysis each week
Apply for mast installation and fault repair jobs
Save 100 pounds a month once I have a job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to protect jobs and families before anything else. Slow it down. Politicians and company bosses who rushed it should answer. I'd tell friends to hold onto any work they have and not to take on debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm terrified. The design and signal processing work I trained for is thinking work, and by 2028 it's done by AI at a fraction of the cost. I'd have a loan with no entry-level jobs to match it, and a wedding to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding, because I couldn't marry on a loan with no job. I'd take any work that pays, even in a warehouse, and keep applying. I'd also ask my parents if I can stay home a few more years, which I hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the kind of fear I can't hide at home. My mother would see it in my face and say a prayer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years leaves your wedding right in the middle of this. What happens to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lucia we put it back a year or two, but we're still going to do it. She'd say fine, because she's a nurse and has seen worse. I'd feel ashamed, though, and I'd have to say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is to blame in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the people who hurried it, the big firms and the ones who write the rules. Not the engineers, who mostly want to build things. And maybe a little, the schools that told us to study this.

say: I'd say we must **protect jobs and families** first, and the people who rushed this should answer for it.
I'd tell friends to hold onto any work and **avoid new debts**.
think: The design work I trained for is thinking work, and AI does it by **2028**.
I'd have a **loan** with no entry-level jobs and a wedding to pay for.
do: **Postpone** the wedding rather than marry on a loan with no job.
Take **any paid work**, even a warehouse job, while still applying.
Ask my parents if I can **stay home** a few more years.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a fear I can't hide at home.
S2.quote: I'd postpone the wedding, because I couldn't marry on a loan with no job.
fieldNote: The scenario hits his **life plans**, not only his job.
Blames the firms and rule-makers who hurried it, not engineers.
Feels shame at the idea of delaying the wedding and living at home.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding by a year or two and tell Lucia first
Take any paid work, even in a warehouse, while applying
Ask my parents if I can stay at home a few more years
Cancel all spending except train fare and loan payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare, so let's use it. Firms should be training young people now, and the government should get out of the way of small businesses that want to hire. I'd say it to anyone, even my uncle at Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious but there's room for a plan. By 2031 I'd have a few years of work, a wedding behind me and some of the loan paid. The design work goes, but I'd know it and plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job at Northlink or a contractor within a year, marry Lucia in two, and put half of every bonus on the loan. I'd learn mast and fibre work, which is physical and lasts longer. And I'd start a savings pot for a deposit, even a small one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, though a long way from calm. I feel like someone standing on a platform and hearing a train that isn't here yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, is the wedding back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably in two years, a smaller one. The date would be set against the job start. It wouldn't be the wedding we dreamed of, but it would be ours, and I'd rather have it ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the loan in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of every bonus and a third of each pay cheque, so I'm clear in six or seven years. And then I'd feel free to take a risk, like a move or a small business with my father.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare, so **firms should train** young people now.
I'd say government should **get out** of the way of small businesses that want to hire.
think: There's room for a plan: some **work years**, a wedding and part of the loan paid by 2031.
The design work goes, but I'd **know** it and plan for it.
do: Get a job at **Northlink** or a contractor within a year.
**Marry Lucia** in two years, in a smaller ceremony.
Learn **mast and fibre work**, which stays physical.
feel: **Better**, but far from calm, like hearing a train that isn't here yet.
S3.quote: I feel like someone standing on a platform and hearing a train that isn't here yet.
fieldNote: Time lets him keep the **wedding** in the plan, at a smaller scale.
Plans a physical skill, mast and fibre work, as insurance.
Business with his father is a first sign of his steady appetite for risk.

steps.text: Get a job at Northlink or a contractor within a year
Marry Lucia in two years with a smaller ceremony
Learn mast and fibre installation work
Put a third of each pay cheque on the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the decade to rebuild apprenticeships and to help families get ahead through work. I'd tell young people not to be afraid, but to prepare. It's a long time, and the people who plan will do fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm comfortable. I'd have a career, a house with Lucia and probably a child or two. The big changes come near the end, and I'd have adapted by then. It's not a perfect position, but it's a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, clear the loan, marry and buy a small house in Ferrow. I'd use the AI tools regularly and take courses on the newest systems. I'd also help my father start a small electrical business, since he knows the trade and I'd know the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. A bit like looking at a long road with a good view. I'd probably get a little cocky, and Lucia would tell me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what does a good life look like for you and Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools earlier, instead of waiting until they're proven. And I'd talk to my father about the business plan now, not later. A decade is only long if you start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything you do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house in Ferrow, a child learning to ride a bike and my father fixing wiring on a job he chose. That's it. That's my idea of a good life.

say: I'd say the decade should be used to **rebuild apprenticeships** and help families get ahead through work.
I'd tell young people to **prepare**, not fear.
think: I'd have a **career**, a house with Lucia and probably a child or two.
The big changes come late, and I'd have **adapted** by then.
do: Clear the **loan**, marry and buy a small house in Ferrow.
Use **AI tools** regularly and take courses on the newest systems.
Help my father start a small **electrical business**.
feel: **Hopeful**, like looking at a long road with a good view.
S4.quote: A house in Ferrow, a child learning to ride a bike and my father fixing wiring on a job he chose.
fieldNote: With a decade his hopes are **concrete**: house, child, father's business.
Wants to start earlier with the tools, a shift from his usual steady pace.
Uneasy, not calm, because early debt still shadows the plan.

steps.text: Clear the loan, marry Lucia and buy a small house in Ferrow
Take courses on the newest telecom systems each year
Help my father start a small electrical contracting business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits just as Lucia and I are starting out. What would help is training placements with real companies, tax relief for firms that hire graduates, and some patience on the loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my father. My father taught me that a man is what he does, and I'm afraid of a world where nobody needs what a person does. I don't know what I'd tell him then.

headlineQuote: My father taught me that a man is what he does, and I'm afraid of a world where nobody needs what a person does.
portrait: Pedro is a **24-year-old** top electrical engineering graduate doing a master's in telecoms, living with his parents in Ferrow.
He is engaged to Lucia, a nurse, and his **wedding plans** shift with every scenario.
He holds traditional views: work over handouts, family and pride in a trade, like his father the electrician.
He uses AI tools **now and then** and plans to use them more as they prove themselves.
His mood is **anxious** to alarmed in the fast worlds and uneasy only with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because it hits as he and Lucia are starting out, with debt.
whatWouldHelp: **Training placements**, tax relief for firms hiring graduates and patience on the loan.
